strengths: Unifying Continuous-Time Perspective: The manuscript offers a clear conceptual view that bridges diffusion models, consistency trajectory models (CTMs), and flow matching via continuous-time ODE solution maps, formulating policy generation as learning the full trajectory map.

Addressing Practical Offline RL Hurdles: The paper identifies key bottlenecks of deploying trajectory-based generative models in RL—specifically inner-loop ODE solver costs and bootstrapping instability—and introduces a closed-form score surrogate along with advantage-weighted policy improvement.

Strong Empirical Results on AntMaze: On the challenging D4RL AntMaze domain, GTP achieves impressive performance (e.g., 80.6 average score, achieving 100 on antmaze-umaze), substantially outperforming standard Diffusion-QL and Consistency-AC baselines.

Thorough Ablation Studies: The ablations in Section 5.3 and Appendix D (evaluating score approximation against full ODE solvers, comparing advantage weighting against linear Q-loss actor objectives, and testing teacher-free alternatives like Shortcut and Mean Flows) provide useful practical insight into why naive continuous-time generative methods struggle in RL.
weaknesses: Incremental Novelty of Core Theoretical Components: While the synthesis is well-executed, several theoretical pieces are largely restatements of existing results: Theorem 2 is the well-established Advantage-Weighted Regression / Boltzmann optimal policy derivation (e.g., REPS, Peters et al., 2010; AWR, Peng et al., 2019; AWAC, Nair et al., 2020) directly applied to a generative loss; and the solution map formulation closely follows Consistency Trajectory Models (Kim et al., 2024).

Discrepancy Between Theorem 1 and Actual Implementation: Theorem 1 analyzes an order-$p$ numerical solver with maximum step size $h$, showing that substituting $\tilde{f}$ incurs an error of $O(h^p)$ as $h \to 0$. However, in Algorithm 1 and Eq. (17), no numerical ODE integration is performed; intermediate states are simply sampled along straight-line noise interpolations ($a_t = a + t \cdot z, \tilde{a}_u = a + u \cdot z$). The theoretical setup in Theorem 1 thus does not directly describe the actual single-step perturbation used in the algorithm.

Missing Benchmark Domains Mentioned in Text: The caption of Table 4 explicitly states: 'The hyperparameters in offline (including BC, $\eta=0$) training on D4RL Gym, AntMaze, Adroit and Kitchen tasks.' However, neither the main paper nor the appendix reports empirical results on Adroit or Kitchen benchmarks. Given that Adroit and Kitchen are standard, complex multi-modal/sparse offline RL benchmarks, their omission despite being referenced raises questions regarding completeness.

Nuance in the Efficiency vs. Expressiveness Trade-off: A primary motivation of the paper is bridging the gap between fast consistency models and expressive diffusion models. However, Table 5 shows that at $T=5$, GTP takes 0.94 ms per step compared to 1.16 ms for Diffusion ($T=5$) and 0.55 ms for Consistency Models ($T=2$). While GTP outperforms Consistency Models in score, it remains ~1.7$\times$ slower, and is only marginally faster than diffusion policies running with the same number of sampling steps.

strengths: Principled Unifying Perspective: The paper provides a coherent framework viewing diffusion models, consistency models, and flow matching through the lens of continuous-time ODE solution maps, which cleanly motivates Generative Trajectory Policies (GTPs) in offline RL.

Practical and Stable Training Formulation: By replacing fragile, computationally prohibitive inner-loop ODE integration with an analytical surrogate anchored to offline samples (with theoretical asymptotic convergence bounds provided in Theorem 1), the method resolves major training instabilities associated with training trajectory models from scratch.

Strong Empirical Performance: GTP achieves competitive results across D4RL locomotion tasks and exhibits particularly impressive gains on the challenging AntMaze suite (e.g., achieving 80.6 average return in RL and 66.3 in BC, notably outperforming prior generative baselines such as Diffusion-QL, Consistency-AC, and QGPO).

Thorough Analysis and Ablations: The manuscript is well supported by extensive appendices covering the theoretical proof of Theorem 1, deep connections to Shortcut Models and Mean Flows, runtime comparisons, and ablations verifying the fragility of alternative teacher-free objectives.
weaknesses: Incremental Novelty in Core Algorithmic Components: While the overarching trajectory formulation is neat, the key building blocks are largely adapted from prior literature. Sampling intermediate points along the linear perturbation path $x_u = x + u \cdot z$ is essentially the standard conditional path coupling used in Consistency Training (Song et al., 2023) and Flow Matching, and exponential advantage weighting (Theorem 2) is well established in offline RL (e.g., AWR, AWAC, IDQL, and recent value-weighted diffusion works).

Missing Baseline Numbers in Table 2: In the AntMaze benchmark in Table 2, multiple tasks (medium-diverse, large-play, large-diverse) for recent generative baselines like BDM and C-AC are left blank ('-'). It would strengthen the evaluation to clarify whether these methods failed/diverged or whether official results were unavailable.

Minor Inconsistency in Algorithm 1: In Algorithm 1, Line 8 states 'Update actor $\Phi_\theta$ using the weighted loss in Eq. (18)', but Eq. (18) is only the instantaneous flow loss $\mathcal{L}_{Flow}$, omitting $\mathcal{L}_{Consistency}$ and the combined objective $\mathcal{L}_{actor}$ defined right below Eq. (18).

Inference Speed Claim Nuance: In Table 5, GTP with $T=5$ is reported as slightly faster (0.94 ms) than Diffusion Policy with $T=5$ (1.16 ms). Because both methods execute 5 forward passes through a neural network, this small delta appears to stem from minor differences in neural network architectures or hyperparameter dimensions rather than an inherent algorithmic reduction in sampling complexity at equal step counts.

strengths: Principled motivation: The paper articulates a clear and conceptually unified perspective connecting diffusion models, consistency models, and flow matching through continuous-time ODE solution maps, motivating the use of Generative Trajectory Policies (GTP) in offline RL.

Strong empirical performance on D4RL: Across standard benchmarks—most notably the challenging AntMaze domains—GTP achieves state-of-the-art results both as a behavior cloner (GTP-BC) and as an actor-critic algorithm (GTP), significantly outperforming existing diffusion and consistency baselines.

Practical training adaptations: The use of an analytical surrogate target to bypass inner-loop multi-step ODE solver integration successfully stabilizes training and avoids severe computational bottlenecks, as supported by training time ablations.

Comprehensive ablations: The authors provide thoughtful ablation experiments comparing teacher-guided vs. teacher-free formulations (Shortcut and Mean Flows) and inspecting inference latency vs. generation quality.
weaknesses: Overstated novelty of theoretical contributions: Theorem 2 and the advantage-weighted objective are essentially standard formulations from prior offline RL literature (such as AWR, AWAC, and Q-weighted diffusion policies), derived directly from KL-constrained policy optimization. Presenting this as a core theoretical contribution of the paper overclaims novelty.

Discrepancy between Theorem 1 and practical implementation: Theorem 1 analyzes multi-step numerical integration of the surrogate vector field $\tilde{f}$, yet Remark 1 and the actual implementation (Eq. 17) bypass the solver altogether by taking a single-step Gaussian perturbation $a_u = a + u \cdot z$. The theoretical analysis and practical implementation are somewhat disconnected.

Missing evaluation domains mentioned in the text: In Table 4 caption, the manuscript references hyperparameters for 'D4RL Gym, AntMaze, Adroit and Kitchen tasks', yet nowhere in the main text or appendix are experimental results on Adroit or Franka Kitchen reported.

Typo and oversight in Algorithm 1: Line 8 of Algorithm 1 states 'Update actor $\Phi_\theta$ using the weighted loss in Eq. (18)', which refers only to the instantaneous flow loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow}}$, omitting the trajectory consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Consistency}}$ and the combined objective $\mathcal{L}_{\text{actor}}$ described in Section 4.3.

Modest inference speedup over diffusion: In the latency benchmark (Table 5), GTP at $T=5$ takes 0.94 ms compared to 1.16 ms for a 5-step diffusion policy, indicating that the runtime efficiency gains over few-step diffusion policies are incremental.

strengths: Principled and cohesive framework: The paper provides a clear and unifying perspective connecting diffusion, flow matching, consistency models, and consistency trajectory models (CTMs) as learning the solution map of a continuous-time ODE, offering a clean conceptual foundation for policy modeling in offline RL.

Theoretically supported and practical training adaptations: The use of an analytical surrogate score field $\tilde{f}(x_t, t) = (x_t - x)/t$ bypasses expensive inner-loop ODE integration and bootstrapping instabilities during training. Theorem 4.1 rigorously establishes an $O(h^p)$ bound on the discrepancy between the practical and ideal training objectives.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated on standard D4RL locomotion and AntMaze benchmarks, demonstrating substantial improvements over previous generative policies (notably on AntMaze, achieving an average score of 80.6). The authors also include evaluations on OGBench and visual control tasks, showing generalizability beyond simple low-dimensional benchmarks.

Thorough ablation and efficiency analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations analyzing sampling horizons ($K=2$ vs. $K=5$), time-scheduling schemes, advantage-weighting vs. linear Q-actor losses, and teacher-based vs. teacher-free training objectives (Shortcut / Mean Flow variants), accompanied by wall-clock training and inference time profiling.
weaknesses: Incremental policy improvement mechanism: The policy improvement framework relies on standard exponential advantage weighting / weighted behavior cloning (Theorem 4.4), which is well-established in offline RL (e.g., REPS, AWR, AWAC, CRR) and has been previously combined with diffusion/generative models. While effective, the algorithmic contribution on the RL optimization side is relatively standard.

Close heritage to prior generative trajectory modeling: The core generative architecture heavily mirrors Consistency Trajectory Models (Kim et al., 2024) and straight-line flow consistency training. While adapting this specifically to an actor-critic framework is valuable, the generative modeling framework itself is largely an adaptation of CTMs and Flow Matching rather than an entirely new generative paradigm.
Incomplete placeholder in the manuscript: At the end of Section 1 (page 2), the repository link is left incomplete ('Our code is publicly available at').

Evaluation metric aggregation: For D4RL benchmark results, reporting Aggregate metrics like Interquartile Mean (IQM) and performance profiles across tasks following standard evaluation protocols (e.g., rliable) would provide a more robust statistical assessment than raw arithmetic means.

strengths: Unifying theoretical perspective: The paper provides a clear and principled framing that connects diffusion models, flow matching, consistency models, and consistency trajectory models under a single ODE flow-map formulation for offline RL policies.

Theoretically supported and practical adaptations: To overcome the instability and cost of learning ODE flow maps from scratch without a pretrained teacher, the authors introduce a closed-form score surrogate anchored to data samples and theoretically prove an asymptotic error bound of $O(h^p)$ (Theorem 4.1).

Strong empirical performance: Across standard D4RL benchmarks (Gym and AntMaze), GTP outperforms both iterative diffusion baselines (Diffusion-QL) and few-step baselines (Consistency-AC), setting strong results especially on the challenging AntMaze suite (average score of 80.6 vs. 69.6 for D-QL and 78.3 for QGPO).

Favorable inference and training efficiency: With only $K=2$ to $K=5$ sampling steps at test time, GTP matches or exceeds diffusion policy performance while maintaining an inference latency of under 1 ms and a training duration (~3.8–4.3 hours) comparable to or faster than existing diffusion and flow-based RL baselines.

Thorough ablation and supplementary evaluation: The paper features extensive analyses, including evaluations on OGBench (both state and visual tasks), detailed comparisons against recent 2025/2026 baselines (FQL, SSCQL, QIPO), sensitivity studies over horizon $T$ and temperature $\eta$, and ablations justifying why alternative teacher-free objectives (e.g., Mean Flows, Shortcut Models) struggle in offline RL.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the value-guidance objective: Theorem 4.4 and the exponential advantage weighting formulation are well-established in the offline RL literature (e.g., REPS, AWAC/AWR, and Q-weighted diffusion policies). Presenting this as a core theoretical contribution slightly overstates its originality in the context of offline RL.

Reliance on prior CTM parameterization: The core parameterization of the flow surrogate $\phi(x_t, t, s)$ is directly adopted from Consistency Trajectory Models (Kim et al., 2024); the paper's primary algorithmic novelty lies in the training adaptations (score approximation and advantage weighting) rather than the flow map representation itself.
Incomplete anonymous repository link: Page 2 ends with an incomplete sentence ('Our code is publicly available at'), leaving out the repository URL or anonymous link.

Hyperparameter sensitivity across domains: As indicated in Appendix Table 4, the advantage temperature $\eta$, max Q backup, and gradient norm clipping require different settings across task families (e.g., $\eta=1.0$ on hopper-medium and antmaze-umaze-diverse vs. $\eta=5.0$ elsewhere), suggesting that hyperparameter tuning remains necessary for optimal performance across varied dataset distributions.

strengths: Unifying perspective: The paper provides a clear conceptual framework that views diffusion models, flow matching, consistency models, and consistency trajectory models through the unified lens of learning continuous-time ODE solution maps, clarifying how these paradigms relate to policy representations in RL.

Well-grounded practical adaptations: The closed-form score approximation replaces expensive multi-step numerical ODE integration during training with an analytical surrogate anchored to the dataset samples, supported by theoretical analysis (Theorem 4.1) proving an O(h^p) approximation bound.

Thorough and competitive empirical evaluation: GTP achieves state-of-the-art results on D4RL (especially on AntMaze, where it significantly outperforms prior generative policies), and the authors provide extensive additional evaluations including comparisons with recent baselines (FQL, QIPO, SSCQL), OGBench, and visual-observation tasks.

Comprehensive ablations and efficiency analysis: The paper thoroughly ablates inference sampling steps (showing K=2 performs comparably to K=5), training time vs. inference latency trade-offs, advantage weighting versus linear Q-guidance, and teacher-based versus teacher-free formulations.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is largely an assembly of existing techniques: The core parameterization of the solution map is directly drawn from Consistency Trajectory Models (Kim et al., 2024), the straight-line perturbation surrogate mirrors Consistency Training and Flow Matching, and the value guidance utilizes standard advantage-weighted regression (AWR/AWAC). While the combination is well-executed and effective for offline RL, the individual technical ingredients are largely established.

Missing repository link and reproducibility detail: Section 1 ends with an incomplete sentence ('Our code is publicly available at'), leaving out the repository URL or anonymous link. Furthermore, the selection mechanism for time triplets (t, u, τ) in Algorithm 1 relative to the dynamic timestep schedule N(k) described in Appendix C.2 could be made clearer in the main text.

Discussion of pure BC performance on AntMaze: In Table 1, GTP-BC achieves remarkably high scores on AntMaze (e.g., 85.0 on antmaze-md and 74.4 on antmaze-mp) without any value-based guidance, substantially outperforming earlier generative BC methods. Given that AntMaze datasets contain mostly undirected, suboptimal play, a deeper discussion or diagnostic on why learning the full ODE solution map facilitates such strong performance in the pure imitation regime would strengthen the paper.

Comparison with linear Q actor loss: In Section 5.3 and Table 3, the linear Q actor baseline is reported to diverge for λ ∈ {0.1, 1.0}. However, existing methods like Diffusion-QL successfully optimize a linear combination of generative loss and Q-maximization. Clarifying whether gradient clipping, Q-normalization, or specific hyperparameter ranges were matched to Diffusion-QL would make this ablation comparison fairer.
